title: From joint-act hypothesis: images share the exemplar's cult genus—dulia, hyperdulia, even latria
source_text: LVI. Porro ex hac hypothesi, quod imago possit & debeat, uno eodemque adorationis actu cum exemplari ipso coli, sequitur, imagines coli posse & debere eodem genere cultus, quo colitur ipsum exemplar. Ac proinde sanctorum imagines coli posse dulia, qui est cultus sanctis peculiaris: Imagines vero Beatae Virginis coli posse hyperdulia, qui cultus est ipsi proprius; ac tandem imagines Dei Christique coli posse latria, qui cultus est Deo debitus; quod etiam fatentur & docent cum Thoma Aquinate plerique Scholastici.
pass_a_gloss: Further, from this hypothesis, that the image can and ought to be cultivated by one and the same act of adoration with the exemplar itself, it follows that images can and ought to be cultivated with the same genus of cult with which the exemplar itself is cultivated. And accordingly the images of the saints can be cultivated with dulia, which is the cult peculiar to the saints: But the Images of the Blessed Virgin can be cultivated with hyperdulia, which cult is proper to her; and finally the images of God and of Christ can be cultivated with latria, which cult is owed to God; which also with Thomas Aquinas most of the Scholastics grant and teach.
pass_b_english: If one act covers image and exemplar, images share the exemplar's cult genus.
Saints' images: dulia; Mary's: hyperdulia; God's and Christ's: latria—as Aquinas and most Scholastics teach.

lemmas.gloss: with the same genus of cult

choices.why: The joint-act premise driving the latria conclusion.
